rule: Questions fixed before any corpus search. Key points come only from the thread's accepted answer or answers scoring >= 10 (local Stack Exchange extract, answers truncated at ~2,000 chars); each cites its answer id. intended_domains is the coverage plan, not a label.

questions.query: Why is processing a sorted array faster than processing an unsorted array?

key_points.text: The slowdown is branch misprediction: the CPU guesses the outcome of the if-branch and must flush the pipeline when wrong.
Predictors use past branch history; on sorted data the condition is a long run of false then true, so it is predictable; on random data it is not.
A branchless form (conditional move / ternary, cmov) removes the penalty and makes timing independent of data order.
Compiler loop transformations (interchange, hoisting the invariant condition) can remove the branch from the hot loop.

questions.query: How to securely hash passwords? If I hash passwords before storing them in my database, is that sufficient to prevent them being recovered?

key_points.text: Hashing is a second line of defence: a read-only breach lets an attacker run an offline dictionary/brute-force attack, which cannot be prevented, only made expensive.
Use a unique per-user salt (stored with the hash) to defeat rainbow tables and parallel cracking of many hashes.
Use a deliberately slow, tunable password-hashing function (bcrypt, PBKDF2, scrypt; later Argon2), not a single fast hash like MD5/SHA-1.
Memory-hard functions (scrypt, Argon2) raise the cost of GPU/hardware attacks; iteration counts must rise as hardware improves.
A pepper (application-held secret) can help when only the database is compromised.

questions.query: Why do we need a TCP 3-way handshake? Why not just 2-way?

key_points.text: Each side picks a random Initial Sequence Number (ISN) and the other must acknowledge it, because TCP is bidirectional.
That is four events (SYN, ACK, SYN, ACK); the middle two are combined into one SYN-ACK packet, giving three.
A two-way handshake would establish only one side's ISN, so only one side could reliably send data.
Each side must get proof its packets reach the other (SYN requests proof, ACK provides it).

questions.query: What's the difference between a binary search tree and a binary heap? What are the time complexities for different operations of each?

key_points.text: Heap order is top-down (parent >= children for max-heap); BST order is left-to-right (in-order sorted).
Heap: find-min/max O(1), insert/delete O(log n), average insert O(1), arbitrary search O(n), build O(n).
Balanced BST: search/insert/delete O(log n); supports sorted order and arbitrary search; build O(n log n).
They implement different abstract types: heap = priority queue, BST = ordered set/map; a heap is a complete tree stored efficiently in an array.

questions.query: When should I use a unique constraint instead of a unique index?

key_points.text: A unique constraint is enforced by a unique index under the hood; the optimizer can use either the same way.
The choice mainly signals intent: constraint for a business rule, explicit index when the column is searched/sorted.
Declaring both creates duplicate indexes that waste space and slow writes.
Engine-specific differences (SQL Server): only an index can be filtered, include columns, or be disabled; foreign keys cannot reference a filtered unique index.

questions.query: Should we MAC-then-encrypt or encrypt-then-MAC (or encrypt-and-MAC) when combining a standalone cipher and a MAC?

key_points.text: Encrypt-then-MAC gives ciphertext integrity: forged ciphertexts are rejected before decryption, which blocks chosen-ciphertext attacks such as padding oracles.
MAC-then-encrypt and encrypt-and-MAC are not generically secure (Krawczyk); encrypt-and-MAC can leak plaintext information via the MAC.
Authenticate-then-encrypt is secure only with CBC mode or a stream cipher (Krawczyk's positive result); SSL uses AtE, SSH E&A, IPsec EtA.
Encrypt-then-MAC must cover the IV and algorithm identifiers, or an attacker can alter them undetected (Ferguson & Schneier's IPsec example).
Doom principle: performing any cryptographic operation before verifying the MAC leads to attacks.

questions.query: Why is quicksort better than other sorting algorithms in practice, despite its O(n^2) worst case?

key_points.text: Cache efficiency: quicksort scans and partitions linearly, using every loaded cache line; heapsort jumps around memory.
Its inner loops (crossing pointers) are very small, so the most-executed code is cheap; exact average-case constants (Knuth, Sedgewick) favour quicksort.
With random pivots, bad splits are rare; even frequent poor splits still give O(n log n).
O-notation hides constants and depends on the input model; average case assumes random permutations.
Adaptive hybrids such as Timsort can beat plain quicksort on real data.

questions.query: Why is it recommended to run only one process in a container?

key_points.text: One function per container makes horizontal scaling, reuse and portability easier.
Components can be patched, upgraded, deployed and rolled back independently; images stay smaller.
Separate containers allow network-level security isolation (e.g. compliance such as PCI).
The runtime monitors only the main process: a crashed secondary process goes unnoticed, and zombie processes may not be reaped without a proper init.
Interleaved stdout makes docker logs hard to use; containers derive from OS-level isolation (chroot lineage) of a single process's libraries, ports and filesystem.
The modern guidance is one concern per container, not literally one process.

questions.query: Why do cost functions use the square error?

key_points.text: Summing raw residuals fails: positive and negative errors cancel, so it can be driven to minus infinity; the sign must be removed.
Squared error corresponds to maximum-likelihood estimation under Gaussian noise, justified by the Central Limit Theorem.
Absolute error (L1) also removes the sign but is not differentiable at zero; squared error has a convenient derivative (hence the 1/2).
The 1/m (mean) makes the loss comparable across sample sizes, suits stochastic mini-batches and keeps regularizer weights stable.

questions.query: CAP theorem: what are Availability and Partition tolerance, and what is the difference between them?

key_points.text: Definitions: consistency = every read sees the latest write; availability = every non-failed node answers; partition tolerance = the system keeps working when nodes cannot communicate.
During a partition you must choose: let nodes diverge (give up consistency, AP) or refuse requests (give up availability, CP).
'Pick 2 of 3' is misleading: partitions are not optional in a distributed system, so CA is effectively a single-node system.
Without a partition you can have both; AP systems face inconsistent reads and write conflicts needing resolution (Brewer's 'CAP twelve years later').

questions.query: What's the difference between Paxos and W+R>N quorums in Cassandra/Dynamo-style systems?

key_points.text: Quorum writes are not atomic across nodes: during a write or after failures some replicas hold new and others old values, so reads can disagree (eventual consistency, repaired later).
Paxos guarantees non-faulty nodes never disagree on a write's outcome, at the cost of delaying or refusing requests when too many nodes fail.
They solve different problems: Paxos is a replicated log / state machine; W+R>N implements a shared register.
Each can in principle implement the other, but inefficiently; practical quorum implementations often weaken guarantees for latency.
The failure models differ: Paxos handles dropped messages and crash-restart; many quorum implementations assume weaker failures.

questions.query: How to ensure that an optimising compiler will terminate, when its rewrite rules could loop forever?

key_points.text: The root problems are the cost model (knowing what is faster) and monotonicity (good optimisations may need temporarily worse steps).
Practical bounds: timeouts or limits on the number of rewrites (the latter keeps builds reproducible).
Canonicalisation: remove redundant forms from the IR (e.g. no shifts in the IR; choose them at instruction selection) so rules cannot bounce between equivalents.
Equality saturation with e-graphs represents all equivalent rewrites at once, reaching a fixed point, then extracts the best term by a cost heuristic.

questions.query: What is the surface code in the context of quantum error correction?

key_points.text: Surface codes are a family of quantum error-correcting codes on a 2D lattice of qubits, differing in boundary conditions: toric code (periodic) and planar code (open boundaries).
They are stabilizer codes: plaquette operators (XXXX) and star/vertex operators (ZZZZ) all commute.
The codespace is the joint +1 eigenspace of all stabilizers; counting independent stabilizers gives the number of logical qubits.
The planar variant is the most realistic for practical large-scale quantum computation.

questions.query: What is the actual time complexity of Gaussian elimination, given that intermediate numbers can grow to exponentially many bits?

key_points.text: The O(n^3) count is arithmetic operations; bit complexity depends on the size of intermediate numbers, which careless elimination lets grow exponentially.

Edmonds: every number computed is a determinant of a submatrix of A, and subdeterminants need at most about twice A's bit length (Schrijver, Theorem 3.2), so with common factors cancelled the algorithm is polynomial.
Bound: O~(n^3 log(||A|| + ||b||)), via Dixon's p-adic expansion method (also Eberly et al., ISSAC'06).

questions.query: How can a language whose compiler is written in C ever be faster than C?

key_points.text: The compiler's implementation language is unrelated to the speed of the code it emits; output quality depends on the compiler's algorithms.
Interpreters differ: they run alongside the program; JIT/hybrid runtimes (JVM, PyPy) can exceed their host language using runtime information.
Language semantics enable optimisations, e.g. Fortran forbids pointer aliasing where C needs restrict.
A JIT can use host-specific instructions and hot-path profiling unavailable to ahead-of-time generic binaries.
Languages are not inherently fast or slow, implementations are; bootstrapping compilers in C is routine; the full employment theorem means optimisation never ends.
